strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: editing an image toward a desired emotional response using only the source image and an emotion label. Several examples demonstrate contextual changes beyond color or style transfer.

EmoPair offers a potentially useful training resource comprising approximately 338,000 pairs. The manuscript identifies the parent datasets and pretrained components and explains the automatic curation pipeline.

The randomized human comparisons provide evidence independent of the emotion classifier. The reported 56% average online preference suggests that the complete system has practical merit against the evaluated baselines.

The figures make the approach accessible, and the supplementary material includes informative failure cases. The manuscript appropriately reports consent, institutional approval, compensation, and risks of emotional manipulation.
weaknesses: The principal quantitative evidence is confounded by evaluator reuse. The same predictor P labels or filters training data, selects outputs over up to 20 editing rounds, and supplies EMR, ESR, and ENRD. EMR drops from 50.20% to 5.06% without this inference procedure (Table 1). Baselines using the same critic and comparable computation, independent classifier evaluation, and human comparisons of the ablations are needed to establish how much the learned editor contributes.

The claimed technical novelty is insufficiently established. The global and local branches largely comprise emotion conditioning and the inherited image diffusion pathway. Because the emotion encoder receives only one of eight fixed labels, its alignment loss learns shared emotion embeddings; this does not substantiate the stronger claims of image-specific, human-like neuro-symbolic reasoning. No controlled comparison isolates the architectural contribution from simpler emotion-conditioned InstructPix2Pix variants.

Baseline coverage leaves important alternatives unresolved. InstructPix2Pix and CLIP-Styler receive single-word emotion prompts, which the manuscript itself explains are ineffective. LMS is a useful stronger comparison, but the closely related Affective Image Filter [30] is discussed without experimental comparison. These omissions weaken claims of superiority over existing emotional editing approaches.

Human evidence supports a narrower conclusion than the manuscript claims. Preference over LMS is 54% online and 49% in the small laboratory study (Fig. S6), with no confidence intervals accounting for repeated participants and images. Only 27% of online participants pass screening, making screening sensitivity and precise retained sample counts important. These results suggest promise but do not establish consistent superiority over the strongest baseline.

Dataset quality is insufficiently validated. Of 338,544 pairs, 331,595 are existing InstructPix2Pix pairs assigned emotions by a classifier reporting 73% accuracy on EmoSet; accuracy on the synthetic pairs is unknown. Human ranking of generic instructions does not validate the resulting image pairs. A human audit of emotion labels and content preservation, plus separate EPAS/EPGS ablations, would establish the resource's reliability and added value.

The evaluation does not adequately establish the joint requirement of emotional change and semantic preservation. Classifier Grad-CAM masks and edge distances provide limited evidence of preserved meaning, while the human task measures only emotional preference. Examples include a lunch box becoming a flower and a tiger becoming rocks. Moreover, Table 1 shows worse ENRD and ESS for the full model than for either ablation, contrary to the accompanying interpretation. Within-valence editing and neutral-image generalization receive only qualitative evaluation.

Important mathematical and implementation details require clarification. ESR is written using KL(prediction || one-hot target), which is infinite for ordinary softmax predictions unless smoothing or a different argument convention is specified. The training description defines the noisy latent from the source image without explaining where the paired target enters the denoising objective. Learning rate, batch size, training duration, emotion-encoder dimensions, and inference sampling settings are also missing. These may be specification errors, but they prevent reliable reproduction and interpretation of the reported results.
